results.result: Histological analysis confirmed that bicuculline injections were localized to the pFL region ventrolateral to the facial nucleus, with no overlap with PHOX2B+ cells in the RTN or TH+ cells in C1/A5 areas. Bicuculline specifically activated disinhibited cells within ~300 μm of injection sites without activating PHOX2B+ cells beyond baseline levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C42 provide converging histological evidence from immunostaining, cell counting, and spatial analysis. The data show specific activation patterns (104.5±5.1 cFos+ cells at injection cores vs 44.7±4.0 in controls) with consistent PHOX2B+/cFos+ counts between groups (2.3±1.0 vs 2.4±0.4), supported by Figure 2A-C. The spatial specificity and lack of RTN activation are well-documented.

results.result: Bicuculline injections consistently elicited ABD recruitment across all tested pFL locations (-0.2 to +0.8 mm from VIIc), but response characteristics varied along the rostro-caudal axis. Rostral locations showed more reliable responses, with unique features including tonic expiratory components and post-I ABD peaks at +0.6/+0.8 mm that were absent at caudal sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C50 describe the basic ABD response patterns with clear experimental evidence. The reliability data (3/5 rats at -0.2 mm vs all rats at rostral sites), EMG characteristics (late-E components across all groups, tonic components only at +0.6/+0.8 mm, post-I peaks in 5/6 rats at +0.6 mm), and airflow deflections are well-documented in the data and Figure 2D. The spatial gradient in response characteristics is consistently demonstrated.

results.result: Temporal analysis revealed that rostral pFL locations (+0.6 and +0.8 mm) produced longer-lasting (17.6±2.7 and 17.1±3.3 min vs 2.4±1.1 min at -0.2 mm), more robust (ABD/DIA coupling 0.89-0.97 vs 0.6), and faster-onset responses (88.7±32.3 s before second injection at +0.6 mm) compared to caudal locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C60 present quantitative temporal dynamics with appropriate statistical support (one-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests, p<0.05). The data show clear rostro-caudal gradients in response duration, coupling strength, and onset latency, supported by Figure 3A-F. The +0.6 mm location's unique early response onset (negative delay values) is particularly well-documented and suggests proximity to the core oscillator.

results.result: Rostral pFL injections (+0.6/+0.8 mm) produced the strongest effects on respiratory parameters: increased tidal volume (29% at +0.6 mm vs 8% at -0.2 mm), increased minute ventilation (16% at +0.6 mm vs -12% at -0.2 mm), with respiratory frequency remaining stable rostrally but dropping significantly at caudal locations (-12% to -17%).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C26, C61-C73 present comprehensive respiratory parameter changes with robust statistical analysis (one-way RM ANOVA, p<0.01, η²=0.44-0.59). The data clearly differentiate rostral from caudal effects, showing that VE changes were frequency-driven caudally but volume-driven rostrally. The timing of peak responses (2-8 min post-injection) and the mechanistic interpretation (increased TE, decreased Ti) are well-supported by Figure 4 and statistical tests.

results.result: Oxygen consumption (VO2) decreased significantly only at rostral injection sites (+0.6 mm: 33% drop, +0.8 mm: 25% drop vs 10-17% at caudal sites), while VE/VO2 ratio increased 73-82% at rostral locations, indicating hyperventilation that was absent at caudal sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 present metabolic consequences with strong statistical support (one-way RM ANOVA, p=0.0001, η²=0.59). The selective decrease in VO2 at rostral sites paired with increased VE clearly demonstrates hyperventilation. The data are internally consistent and supported by Figure 4L-O. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C79-C80) about reduced work of breathing remains speculative without direct measurements.

results.result: Novel area-under-curve (AUC) analysis of individual respiratory phases revealed that rostral injections (+0.6/+0.8 mm) produced significantly stronger alterations in airflow and ABD EMG during late-E, inspiratory, and post-I phases compared to caudal locations, with effects persisting 8-16 min post-injection.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C94 describe results from a novel analytical method with appropriate statistical testing (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's post-hoc, p<0.05). The phase-specific analysis (Figure 5D-F) successfully differentiates rostral from caudal responses across all respiratory phases. The interpretation that ABD contributions during inspiration are negligible (C89) is appropriately justified by the integration artifact explanation. The temporal persistence data strengthen the rostral vs caudal distinction.

results.result: Novel 3D multivariate trajectory analysis differentiated the two rostral locations: +0.8 mm injections produced the strongest late-E 'tails' and post-I 'feet' (6-20 min duration), while +0.6 mm injections produced the most prominent inspiratory 'bulbs' (8-14 min peak), revealing functional heterogeneity within the rostral pFL.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30, C95-C106, C144-C147 present results from a second novel analytical method (3D trajectory mapping with Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances). The statistical support is robust (Kruskal-Wallis tests, p<0.05) and the method successfully discriminates between the two rostral locations that appeared similar in standard analyses. Figure 6 provides clear visual and quantitative support. The interpretation of functional heterogeneity (C147-C148) is reasonable given the phase-specific differences, though mechanistic explanations remain speculative.

results.result: Two novel analytical methods were developed: (1) an AUC algorithm for phase-specific respiratory analysis and (2) a 3D multivariate trajectory mapping approach. These methods enabled more precise characterization of respiratory responses than traditional measures and were robust to in vivo measurement variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C143 describe methodological innovations that are well-documented in the Methods section and Figure 1. The novelty is supported by literature review (C138), and the utility is demonstrated by the ability to detect differences not visible in standard analyses (C144). The claim about robustness to variability (C143) is supported by the Mahalanobis distance approach accounting for cycle-by-cycle variability. These are genuine methodological contributions to respiratory physiology.

results.result: The +0.6 mm location represents the most critical site for active expiration generation based on fastest response onset, while the rostro-caudal organization of pFL is more complex than previously recognized, with functional heterogeneity suggesting distinct neuronal populations at different coordinates that are likely PHOX2B-negative.
results.evaluation: Claims C127, C135, C148, C158-C160 present interpretive conclusions that extend beyond the direct data. While the +0.6 mm location shows fastest onset (C58, well-supported), the claim that it's 'most critical' (C127) conflates response latency with functional importance—the +0.8 mm site shows stronger late-E/post-I effects. The inference about distinct neuronal populations (C148) is reasonable but speculative without cellular characterization. The PHOX2B-negative conclusion (C158) is supported by histology but only for sites rostral to +0.1 mm.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that bicuculline has secondary pharmacological effects beyond GABA-A receptor antagonism, including inhibition of Ca2+-activated K+ currents and potentiation of NMDA currents, which may contribute to the observed responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 appropriately acknowledge a limitation of the pharmacological approach, citing prior work (Johnson and Seutin, 1997). This is a valid technical consideration that doesn't invalidate the spatial mapping results but correctly notes that the mechanism may not be purely GABAergic disinhibition. The cautionary statement is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: Prior literature shows conflicting evidence about the anatomical location of the expiratory oscillator, with some studies pointing to the caudal tip of VIIc (-0.2 to +0.5 mm) and others to more rostral areas (+0.3 to +1.0 mm), with chemogenetic inhibition studies showing incomplete suppression of ABD activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C16-C21 accurately summarize the state of prior literature with appropriate citations. The characterization of the debate is fair and the evidence for incomplete boundaries (C19, C21) is supported by the cited chemogenetic studies showing partial inhibition. This provides appropriate context for the current study's motivation.

results.result: Prior work established temporal correlation between late-E neuron activity and ABD recruitment in response to bicuculline, presence of GABAergic inputs to late-E neurons, and that ABD/DIA coupling indicates response robustness, with bicuculline effects lasting 16-30 min, though rostro-caudal differences in duration were not previously specified.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108, C122-C125 accurately cite and characterize prior research findings that provide context for the current study's measurements. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of gaps in prior work (C125) is accurate. This establishes the foundation for the current study's contributions.

results.result: The current findings on respiratory frequency, tidal volume, and minute ventilation changes are consistent with some prior bicuculline studies at caudal locations, but the study reveals previously unreported differences at rostral locations and suggests the frequency drop at caudal sites may result from Bötzinger complex disinhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C134 compare current results to prior work with appropriate citations. The consistency with prior caudal location studies (C129, C132-C133) is well-supported. However, the Bötzinger complex hypothesis (C131) is speculative without direct evidence—the spatial proximity argument is plausible but alternative explanations aren't excluded. The claim about absence of rostral location studies (C134) may overstate the gap given Silva et al. 2019 studied +0.3 to +1.0 mm.

results.result: The authors speculate that ABD recruitment might facilitate respiratory mechanics in vivo, reducing work of breathing and causing reduced O2 consumption, citing prior work on respiratory mechanics.
results.evaluation: Claim C136 presents a mechanistic hypothesis for the VO2 decrease that is plausible and supported by citations to respiratory mechanics literature. However, this remains speculative without direct measurements of work of breathing, chest wall mechanics, or muscle efficiency. The alternative explanation (hyperventilation-induced metabolic changes) is also presented (C79-C80), showing appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: Background claims establish that pFL generates active expiration via ABD recruitment, preBötC generates inspiratory rhythm, the expiratory oscillator is challenging to locate due to lack of markers and resting inactivity, bicuculline is a GABA-A antagonist widely used to study pFL, and prior studies used presence/absence of active expiration as the primary outcome measure.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C13, C22-C24, C111-C117, C149-C151 present established background knowledge with appropriate citations. These are accurate characterizations of the field that provide context for the study. The observation about limitations of prior methodology (C116-C117) appropriately motivates the current study's more comprehensive approach.

results.result: The mechanisms underlying post-I ABD activity and the functional implications of different ABD response configurations (late-E only vs. late-E plus post-I) remain unknown, though interactions with post-I oscillators or pontine networks may be involved. Future studies should investigate whether rostral and caudal pFL neurons share the same phenotypic and electrical properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121, C152 appropriately identify knowledge gaps and suggest future directions. The acknowledgment that post-I ABD mechanisms are unknown (C119) is accurate, and the speculation about potential circuits (C120) is appropriately tentative. The suggestion for future phenotypic characterization (C152) is reasonable given the functional heterogeneity observed. These represent appropriate scientific discussion of limitations and future work.

results.result: An ongoing debate exists about whether the expiratory oscillator consists of PHOX2B-negative late-E neurons (pFL) or PHOX2B+/NMB+ RTN neurons. While PHOX2B+/NMB+ stimulation can cause ABD activity, these studies lack late-E recordings from PHOX2B+ neurons, whereas PHOX2B-negative late-E neurons are well-documented. The current study's histology shows minimal PHOX2B/cFos+ staining at rostral sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C157 accurately characterize an ongoing scientific debate with appropriate citations to both sides. The critical observation about missing late-E recordings from PHOX2B+ neurons (C155) is a valid methodological point. The histological data (C157) showing minimal PHOX2B activation rostral to +0.1 mm supports the PHOX2B-negative hypothesis for rostral pFL, though this doesn't definitively resolve the broader debate about RTN involvement in active expiration.

results.result: The study used 35 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (340.4±13.2 g) with bilateral pressure injections of 200 µM bicuculline/fluorobeads (200 nl per side at 100 nl/min), following approved animal care protocols.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 describe basic methodological details that are clearly stated and appropriate for the experimental design. Sample size (n=35 total, distributed across groups), injection parameters, and ethical approval are all documented. These are standard methodological details that support reproducibility.

results.result: The authors conclude that bicuculline injections induce complex interactions between DIA and ABD activation across respiratory phases, and that the multidimensional trajectory map will enhance understanding of expiratory oscillator function and provide foundation for future investigations into modulation, plasticity, and therapeutic targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C162 present forward-looking conclusions. The statement about complex interactions (C140) is well-supported by the data. However, the claims about future impact (C161-C162) are speculative—while the methods show promise, their actual utility for future therapeutic development remains to be demonstrated. The enthusiasm is understandable but represents expected rather than demonstrated impact.

results.result: Bicuculline injections at various pFL sites (−0.2 mm to +0.8 mm from VIIc) consistently elicited ABD recruitment, but the response strength, duration, and onset varied along the rostro-caudal axis. The most robust and enduring changes in tidal volume, minute ventilation, and combined respiratory responses occurred at more rostral pFL locations (+0.6/+0.8 mm from VIIc), with the +0.6 mm location showing the fastest response onset.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states the study presents 'solid evidence for a valuable finding of pharmacological mapping' and addresses 'where these regions lie anatomically.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'convincingly show that although bicuculline injections at all coordinates of the pFL generated an expiratory response, the most rostral locations...play the strongest role in generating active expiration.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the data provide novel insights into the importance of rostral locations in controlling active expiration.'

results.result: Multivariate analysis of the respiratory cycle differentiated between locations, revealing distinct features including late-E 'tails', inspiratory 'bulbs', and post-I 'feet'. The strongest deformations of the respiratory loop during late-E and post-I occurred with injections at +0.8 mm, while injections at +0.6 mm produced more pronounced deformations during the inspiratory phase. This novel analytical approach enabled more precise assessment of how targeted stimulation affects particular phases of the respiratory cycle.
results.evaluation: Reviewers 2 and 3 explicitly praise the novel analytical methods. Reviewer 2 states 'Major strengths of this work include...the use of a novel phase-plane analysis' and notes the authors 'construct a comprehensive functional map revealing functional nuances in respiratory responses.' Reviewer 3 emphasizes 'The authors use innovative analytic methods to characterize the respiratory effects of bicuculline injections into various areas of the pFL.' No concerns are raised about the validity of these analytical approaches.

results.result: Histological analysis confirmed that injection sites were positioned ventrolateral to the facial nucleus with no overlap between fluorobead-marked injection sites and PHOX2B+ cells in the RTN, or with TH+ cells in C1/A5 areas. Bicuculline specifically activated disinhibited cells within ~300 μm of injection sites and did not activate PHOX2B+ cells beyond baseline levels, particularly at rostral locations (+0.1 mm and beyond).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms this finding: 'The authors also confirmed histologically that none of the injection sites overlapped grossly with PHOX2B+ neurons, thus confirming the specificity of the injections in the pFL and not the neighboring RTN.' This anatomical confirmation is treated as an important validation of the experimental approach, with no concerns raised about the histological methods or interpretations.

results.result: The elicited ABD response was characterized by a late-E component in the ∫ABD EMG trace and a downward deflection in airflow signifying active expiration across all experimental groups. In the most rostral groups (+0.6 mm and +0.8 mm), the ∫ABD EMG traces exhibited a tonic expiratory component preceding the late-E peak. Area under the curve (AUC) analysis revealed that airflow was substantially altered in all three phases of the respiratory cycle, with effects strongest when targeting rostral areas of the pFL.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states the authors 'convincingly show' that responses at rostral locations 'were characterized by a strong impact on the duration and strength of ABD activation.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'The data provide novel insights into the importance of rostral locations in controlling active expiration.' The detailed characterization of ABD responses across respiratory phases is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Bicuculline injection induced changes in respiratory parameters including frequency, tidal volume (VT), minute ventilation (VE), and oxygen consumption (VO2). The drop in respiratory frequency was significant only in the two most caudal groups. VT increased in all locations except −0.2 mm, with the peak at +0.6 mm. VE increased at rostral locations but decreased at the most caudal location. VO2 dropped only at the most rostral sites (+0.6 mm and +0.8 mm), and the VE/VO2 ratio increased only at these two rostral locations, suggesting hyperventilation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes that responses at rostral locations were 'characterized by...a robust change in tidal volume and minute ventilation,' explicitly affirming these findings. Reviewer 3 confirms 'The results indicate that injections at more rostral pFL locations induce the most robust changes in tidal volume, minute ventilation, and combined respiratory responses.' No reviewer questions the validity of these respiratory parameter measurements or their interpretation.

results.result: Responses had shorter duration in the most caudal locations (−0.2 mm; +0.1 mm; +0.4 mm) compared to rostral locations (+0.6 mm; +0.8 mm). The ABD response initiated following the second bicuculline injection in all groups except at +0.6 mm, where it commenced following the first injection. The coupling of ∫ABD EMG and ∫DIA EMG peak signals was notably weaker at the most caudal location compared to rostral groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly affirms that rostral location responses were 'characterized by a strong impact on the duration and strength of ABD activation.' The temporal dynamics and coupling measurements are part of the comprehensive characterization that reviewers praise, with no concerns raised about these specific findings.

results.result: Bicuculline has previously been shown to exhibit inhibitory effects on Ca2+-activated K+ currents and induce nonspecific potentiation of NMDA currents. Therefore, activation of late-E neurons and active expiration may be triggered by secondary pharmacological effects of bicuculline beyond GABAergic disinhibition.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges this limitation: 'Although a caveat of the approach is that bicuculine injections have indiscriminate effects on other neuronal populations in the region (GABAergic, glycinergic, and glutamatergic), the results can largely be interpreted as modulation of neuronal populations in different regions of the pFL have differential effects on expiratory output. This limitation of the pharmacological approach has also been aptly discussed by the authors.' Reviewer 3 similarly notes 'Bicuculline injections increase the excitability of neurons. Aside of blocking GABA receptors, bicuculline also inhibits calcium-activated potassium currents and potentiates NMDA currents, thus insights into the role of GABAergic inhibition are limited.' This represents a recognized methodological limitation rather than a refutation of findings.

results.result: The nuanced effects observed at different rostro-caudal locations may suggest differences in the functional characteristics, phenotypes, and projections of cell populations at specific coordinates within the pFL. Future investigation is needed to determine whether phenotypic and electrical properties of neurons at more rostral positions share the same identity as those at more caudal positions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises a fundamental concern about interpretation: 'Increasing the excitability of neurons provides little insights into the activity pattern and function of the activated neurons. Without recording from the activated neurons, it is impossible to know whether an effect on active expiration or any other respiratory phase is caused by bicuculline acting on rhythmogenic neurons or tonic neurons that modulate respiration.' This indicates that while the functional differences are observed, the mechanistic interpretation regarding distinct cell populations remains uncertain without additional cellular-level data.

results.result: The results highlight the functional diversity of the lateral parafacial region and emphasize the strong role of the most rostral locations in generating active expiration. The novel multidimensional map advanced understanding of the parafacial region and will enhance understanding of the expiratory oscillator's role in respiratory control, providing a foundation for future investigations into modulation, plasticity, and potential therapeutic targets.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Results from these experiments will be of value to those interested in the neural control of breathing and other neuroscientists as a framework for how to perform pharmacological mapping experiments in the future.' Reviewer 2 concludes 'Collectively, these findings advance our understanding of the presumed expiratory oscillator, the pFL, and highlight the functional heterogeneity in the functional response of this anatomical structure.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The study indicates that the rostro-caudal organization of the pFL and its influence on breathing is not simple and uniform,' affirming the significance of the findings despite methodological limitations.
